# Ball radialization can change the centroid direction

The counterexamples below are concave densities on planar rectangles. They
preserve every halfplane mass fraction through the origin under the usual
Ball radial construction, but their full centroids are not positively
proportional. The first example additionally has two independent centered
line sections, which become centered chords of the radial body.

## 1. An exact radial transport for affine densities

For q>0 let

    D_q=[-1,1/2] x [-1,q],
    f_q(x,y)=(1+x) 1_{D_q}(x,y).

On its convex positive support the density is concave and log-concave; it
is therefore a concave-power profile with exponent m=1. Values on the
zero-density face x=-1 do not affect any integral. Its mass is

    M_q=(q+1) integral_{-1}^{1/2}(1+x)dx=9(q+1)/8.

For a unit vector u let R(u) be the radial extent of D_q. Define the Ball
radial body B_q by

    rho_q(u)^2=2 integral_0^infinity r f_q(ru)dr
              =R(u)^2 [1+(2/3)u_x R(u)].                 (1)

Put s(x)=sqrt(1+2x/3) and

    T(x,y)=s(x)(x,y).

For each ray the radial function r -> r s(r u_x) is strictly increasing
in the interior, since its derivative is (1+r u_x)/s(r u_x)>0. Its endpoint
is exactly the square root in (1). Thus T maps D_q onto B_q and is a
bijection on their interiors. Its Jacobian is

    det DT=s(x)[s(x)+x s'(x)]=1+x=f_q(x,y).               (2)

Consequently Lebesgue measure on B_q is the pushforward of f_q(x,y)dxdy.
The map keeps every ray from 0 fixed, so, for every closed halfplane H
through 0,

    |B_q intersect H|/|B_q|=integral_H f_q / M_q.          (3)

Both boundary lines have measure zero. In particular this statement
includes every orientation, not only the two coordinate directions.

For completeness B_q is indeed convex without invoking a general Ball
body theorem. Write X=x s(x), which increases from -1/sqrt(3) to
1/sqrt(3). Let S(X)=s(x(X)). In the interior

    S'(X)=1/[3(1+x(X))],

which is decreasing. Hence S is positive and concave, including its
continuous endpoint values. The transformed body is exactly

    B_q={(X,Y): -1/sqrt(3)<=X<=1/sqrt(3),
                 -S(X)<=Y<=q S(X)}.

Its upper graph is concave and its lower graph is convex.

## 2. Exact centroid integrals

The x marginal has zero first moment:

    integral_{-1}^{1/2} x(1+x)dx=0.

The original centroid is therefore

    g_f=(0,(q-1)/2).                                     (4)

By (2), the centroid of B_q is E_f[T(X,Y)]. Set Z=9/8, the x-marginal
mass. The following two integrals are exact:

    Z^{-1} integral_{-1}^{1/2} x(1+x)s(x)dx
        =8/(105 sqrt(3)),
    Z^{-1} integral_{-1}^{1/2} (1+x)s(x)dx
        =232/(135 sqrt(3)).                              (5)

For verification substitute u=1+2x/3, whose endpoints are 1/3 and 4/3.
For the first integral divided by Z an antiderivative is

    6u^(7/2)/7 - 8u^(5/2)/5 + 2u^(3/2)/3.

For the second integral before division by Z an antiderivative is

    (3/4)[6u^(5/2)/5 - 2u^(3/2)/3].

It follows that

    g_B=(8/(105 sqrt(3)),
         [(q-1)/2] 232/(135 sqrt(3))).                    (6)

## 3. Two independent centered sections, but different centroids

Take q=1. Equations (4) and (6) give

    g_f=(0,0),             g_B=(8/(105 sqrt(3)),0) !=0.

The horizontal section of f is (1+x) on [-1,1/2], whose centroid is 0.
The vertical section is the uniform density 1 on [-1,1], also centered.
Their Ball-body chords have endpoints

    horizontal: (-1/sqrt(3),0), (1/sqrt(3),0),
    vertical:   (0,-1), (0,1).

Thus both original sections and both transformed chords are centered,
and all origin-halfplane fractions agree, while the full centroids do
not agree even in their vanishing. These properties cannot imply
positive scalar alignment of the full centroid vectors.

## 4. Nonzero centroids and strict directional sign reversal

Take q=2. The two centroid vectors are

    g_f=(0,1/2),
    g_B=(8/(105 sqrt(3)),116/(135 sqrt(3))).

They are not parallel. With u=(-12,1),

    u.g_f=1/2>0,
    u.g_B=-52/(945 sqrt(3))<0.

Hence even the sign of an arbitrary full-centroid projection need not
transfer under Ball radialization. The horizontal line section remains
centered in this example; the vertical one is not centered. This strict
sign counterexample concerns unrestricted centroid-direction transfer,
whereas Section 3 is the counterexample retaining two stationary axes.
Neither example disproves a weighted stationary-section cap inequality.

## 5. The zero-centroid obstruction occurs for every positive integer power

The same qualitative failure is not confined to m=1. For m>=1 let

    D_m=[-1,1/(m+1)] x [-1,1],
    f_m(x,y)=(1+x)^m 1_{D_m}(x,y).

Then f_m^(1/m) is affine on its convex positive support, and g_f=0:
writing L=(m+2)/(m+1), its x moment is

    integral_0^L (u-1)u^m du
       =L^(m+2)/(m+2)-L^(m+1)/(m+1)=0.

Set A_m(x)=2 integral_0^1 t(1+t x)^m dt and s_m=sqrt(A_m).
The radial map T_m(x,y)=s_m(x)(x,y) has

    det DT_m=A_m+(x/2)A_m'=(1+x)^m,

by integrating the derivative of t^2(1+t x)^m from 0 to 1. It is the
same exact radial transport to the Ball radial set. Since s_m is strictly
increasing, E_f[X s_m(X)]>0 when E_f[X]=0. Indeed it is the strictly
positive covariance of X and s_m(X), as follows from

    2 Cov(X,s_m(X))
       =E[(X-X')(s_m(X)-s_m(X'))]>0

for independent nonconstant copies X,X'. Thus the transformed centroid
has positive x coordinate. Both coordinate line sections are again
centered, and the radial construction gives centered coordinate chords.
The fully explicit convex-body certificate in Sections 1--4 already
suffices; this extension records the same mean-transport obstruction for
every positive integer concave-power exponent.

## 6. Strict sign reversal normal to a centered section

There is also a strict directional counterexample for the normal of a
line section that is itself centered. Put

    k=199/100,       b=(k^2-3)/2=9601/20000,
    D=[-1,b] x [-1,1],       f=(1+x)1_D.

The same radial map T and Jacobian computation from Section 1 apply;
its image is again convex by the same upper/lower graph argument. The
vertical section x=0 is uniform on [-1,1], and its Ball chord is exactly
that same centered segment. The full centroid has

    g_f,x=(2b-1)/3=-133/10000<0.

To calculate the transformed x centroid define

    A(t)=2t^7/63 - 8t^5/45 + 2t^3/9,
    Z=(1+b)^2/2.

The substitution from Section 2 now has upper endpoint u=k^2/3.
It gives exactly

    sqrt(3) g_B,x=(9/[8Z])[A(k)-A(1)]
                  =16184667199/312903500000>0.

Both y coordinates of the full centroids vanish by reflection symmetry.
Thus even for the normal u=(1,0) of a centered line section, the full
centroid projection can reverse sign after the radial transformation.
This is stronger than the unrestricted sign example in Section 4; it
still does not assert that every other line section is centered.
